title: Filtered Coffee Linked to Slower Biological Aging While Instant Coffee Shows Opposite Effect
excerpt: A UK Biobank study of nearly 50,000 people found divergent associations between coffee brewing types and biological aging markers, with inflammation as a possible mediating pathway
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Filtered coffee is linked to slower biological aging, while instant coffee shows the opposite effect.
  • Instant coffee consumption correlates with 0.1 to 0.2 years of biological age acceleration per intake category.
  • Inflammation, indicated by GlycA, mediates up to 35% of the link between instant coffee and aging.
  • The study's cross-sectional design limits causal conclusions; further research is necessary.

  • A UK Biobank study of nearly 50,000 participants found that filtered coffee consumption was associated with lower biological age-acceleration scores and longer telomeres, while instant coffee showed the opposite pattern.
  • The effects of instant coffee corresponded to roughly 0.1 to 0.2 years of age acceleration per intake category — statistically significant but of marginal clinical significance at the individual level.
  • Glycoprotein acetylation (GlycA), an inflammatory marker, mediated up to 35% of the association between instant coffee and accelerated biological aging, suggesting inflammation as a potential pathway.
  • The study was cross-sectional and cannot establish causation; prospective and intervention studies are needed before results can inform dietary guidelines.

How you brew your coffee may matter as much as how much you drink, according to new research published in npj Science of Food. A study analysing data from nearly 50,000 UK Biobank participants found that filtered coffee consumption was associated with markers of slower biological aging, while instant coffee consumption showed associations with accelerated aging — a divergence that held across multiple measures.

What the Study Measured

Researchers led by Yuxuan Wang examined three biological aging measures: PhenoAge Acceleration and Klemera-Doubal Method Biological Age Acceleration (KDM-BA Accel), both of which quantify biological age based on biochemical and clinical parameters, and relative leukocyte telomere length (rLTL), a marker of cellular aging where shorter telomeres are associated with older biological age.

The 49,414 participants, with an average age of 56.4 years, consumed an average of 0.7 cups of filtered coffee and 1.5 cups of instant coffee daily. About 44% were female, 65% had a history of hypertension, and 23% reported drinking decaffeinated coffee.

Filtered vs. Instant: Divergent Patterns

> **"GlycA mediated 24.6% and 34.6% of the associations between instant coffee consumption and PhenoAge and KDM-BA Acceleration, respectively."**

"GlycA mediated 24.6% and 34.6% of the associations between instant coffee consumption and PhenoAge and KDM-BA Acceleration, respectively."

Compared with non-drinkers, instant coffee intake showed significant overall trends toward increased PhenoAge Acceleration and KDM-BA Acceleration, and lower telomere length — a pattern consistent with faster biological aging. Filtered coffee showed the opposite: decreased age-acceleration scores and generally longer telomeres, consistent with slower aging. No significant trends emerged for other coffee types.

"Filtered coffee was associated with a more favorable biological-aging biomarker profile than instant coffee."

— Wang et al., npj Science of Food, 2026

The authors were careful to note that the instant-coffee effects corresponded to approximately 0.1 to 0.2 years of age acceleration — a difference that is statistically significant but "of marginal clinical significance at the individual level." In other words, switching from instant to filtered coffee is unlikely to make someone measurably younger, but at a population level, the divergence is worth understanding.

Inflammation May Be the Mechanism

Mediation analysis pointed to glycoprotein acetylation (GlycA), an inflammatory biomarker, as a key statistical pathway. GlycA mediated 24.6% and 34.6% of the associations between instant coffee consumption and PhenoAge and KDM-BA Acceleration, respectively. It also mediated a substantial portion of filtered coffee's protective association with these measures.

Cystatin C, a kidney function marker, and basal metabolic rate (BMR) also emerged as mediators for filtered coffee's association with lower age acceleration, explaining 14% to 18% of the effect. None of these mediators explained the telomere-length associations.

Why the Difference?

The study did not directly test mechanisms, but the difference likely comes down to chemistry. Filtered coffee passes through paper or metal filters that remove diterpenes — compounds like cafestol and kahweol that raise cholesterol levels. Instant coffee undergoes industrial processing including spray-drying or freeze-drying, which alters its chemical composition. Previous research has linked instant coffee to higher levels of acrylamide, a compound formed during processing that has been associated with oxidative stress.

Subgroup analyses revealed that among heavy instant coffee drinkers (more than three cups daily), males, people aged 60 and above, and current smokers had particularly elevated biological age acceleration.

Important Caveats

Inflammation's Role in Aging
›GlycA mediates 24.6% of PhenoAge association with instant coffee.
›GlycA mediates 34.6% of KDM-BA association with instant coffee.
›Cystatin C and BMR explain 14% to 18% of filtered coffee's benefits.

The study was cross-sectional, meaning it captured a single snapshot and cannot establish that either coffee type caused changes in biological aging. Coffee intake was self-reported, the study population was predominantly White and from England, and residual confounding cannot be ruled out. Sensitivity analyses — excluding participants with cancer, diabetes, or cardiovascular disease, and those who added sugar, milk, or artificial sweeteners — showed materially unchanged results, but these analyses have inherent limits.

For the many Indian diaspora households where filter coffee is deeply embedded in daily ritual — particularly in South Indian communities — the findings offer modest reassurance. But the researchers are clear: prospective and intervention studies are needed before these results can inform dietary guidelines. For now, the study adds nuance to an old question, suggesting that when it comes to coffee and aging, the brew method deserves as much attention as the cup count.
